Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Comparative single-cell profiling reveals distinct cardiac resident macrophages essential for zebrafish heart regeneration" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1. For revision at the experimental level. the points outlined by the reviewers below would be a good addition

2. Some further bioinformatics analysis should be performed as suggested.

3. The manuscript requires rewriting/reformulating/putting into context.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors define macrophage-depleted zebrafish as "non-regenerating". I don't think is quite accurate. While it is true that these zebrafish do not regenerate as efficiently as those without prior clodronate depletion of macrophages, these zebrafish should more be more accurately as "macrophage depleted" rather than "non-regenerating". The regeneration defect is secondary to macrophage depletion and changes in gene expression do not necessarily reflect the regeneration defect as much as the loss of resident macrophages, which is true even after the number of circulation macrophages has recovered.

The discussion of all the gene expression data in the Results section would likely benefit from some streamlining and focus on more general principles. As it is currently written, it has a lot of detail, which isn't bad necessarily but it makes reading large sections of the Results section quite cumbersome.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall, we think that this paper provides useful information regarding the heterogeneity and transcriptomic behaviour of resident macrophages and neutrophils during regeneration. Regarding the second part of the paper, the pre-depletion of macrophages and assessment of regeneration, the work seems very derivative of the last author work. Although in the current paper, the authors use different timepoint to deplete the population and by that add the information that even very early depletion is sufficient to detrimentally affect regeneration, they do not expand on this point and instead analyse it in the same scope they did in the previous paper. The early pre-depletion result is very surprising as the expectation from resident macrophage (based on studies in mice) is to hold a self-maintaining ability which given sufficient time would partly replenish itself and could help regenerate the heart. In our view focusing more on what leads to a lack of regeneration in this model, would be of great interest.

One of the caveats of this work is that it draws biological conclusions solely based on transcriptomic data. Although this is common practice when working with scRNA seq datasets, a large part of the inferred conclusions could be tested by adding a dimension of "biological certainty" to otherwise suggestive work, however, we believe that this is outside of the scope of this current study.

As a general note, this paper is written in an understandable way, however, the level of details provided in the text for the majority of aspects such as the gene ontology enrichment (Figure 1d, line 261 "At 7 dpci, up-regulated DEGs in both PBS- and CL-treated hearts were associated to "immune/inflammatory response", "chemokine-mediated signaling", "proteolysis", "neutrophil chemotaxis", "phagocytosis", "cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction", and "NOD-like receptor signaling pathway" (7d-Common, Figure 1D and 1E). These processes correspond nicely with known repairing processes of immune cell infiltration and debris clearance in the first week of cardiac repair.") makes the reading of the paper challenging. We would suggest writing in a more concise way while attempting to keep the details (we acknowledge it is not an easy task).

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. I was missing some functional validations of some of the hub genes defining some of the relevant populations. One could though argue that this goes beyond the current article, which already counts with 8 Figures.

2. I was missing a description of Figure 8C (effect on cardiomyocyte proliferation) in the Results section. Also, a longer discussion of this in my point of view very unexpected results is missing. Would it mean that circulating macrophages are important for cardiomyocyte proliferation?

3. As mentioned in the introduction, previous reports describe subpopulations of macrophages involved in zebrafish heart regeneration (e.g. Ma et al. Bevan et al., Sanz-Morejon et al). The marker genes used in those studies are not put into context with the currently presented data in full. For example, which are the populations expressing osteopontin (ssp1) or wt1b?

4. IP injection of chlodronate leads to a reduction of macrophages in the heart. It might however also lead to macrophage ablation elsewhere in the body. Can the authors exclude that the reason why there is a lack of proper regeneration is that a chlodronate-sensitive macrophage population was ablated throughout the organisms, not only in the heart? If not, this possibility should be discussed.

5. It would be interesting to know if the phenotype is a delay in regeneration or a complete abrogation. Could the authors include long-term AFOG stainings, e.g. 100 dpci?

results.result: Bulk RNA-seq analysis revealed that delaying macrophage recruitment by clodronate liposome treatment (−1d_CL) leads to prolonged inflammatory response, disrupted ROS homeostasis, and misregulated energy metabolism in zebrafish hearts until 21 days post-cardiac injury. The transcriptome of non-regenerative CL-treated hearts at 21 dpci resembled PBS-control hearts at 7 dpci, suggesting delayed transcriptomic response. Genes associated with ROS homeostasis, ribosomal subunits, and metabolic processes showed distinct temporal patterns between regenerative and non-regenerative conditions.
results.evaluation: The bulk RNA-seq data with PCA analysis (Figure 1B), hierarchical clustering (Figure 1C), and pathway analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) provide strong convergent evidence for transcriptomic differences between regenerative and non-regenerative conditions. The temporal progression, metabolic gene expression patterns, and inflammatory pathway activation are well-documented with appropriate statistical analysis and biological replicates. The interpretation aligns with established knowledge about cardiac metabolism and inflammation.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq profiling identified 19 distinct inflammatory cell clusters including 9 macrophage subpopulations, 2 neutrophil clusters, and 1 hybrid cluster in zebrafish hearts. These heterogeneous populations showed diverse gene expression patterns associated with phagocytosis, neutrophil recruitment, ROS homeostasis, angiogenesis, ECM remodeling, and inflammatory regulation. FACS analysis confirmed the presence of resident macrophages (~0.6% of cardiac cells) that proliferate locally and populate the injury site after cardiac injury.
results.evaluation: The scRNA-seq data with UMAP visualization (Figure 2B), marker gene expression (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), and FACS validation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) provide robust evidence for cellular heterogeneity. The clustering is supported by established lineage markers (spi1b, coro1a, mpeg1, mpx) and validated by multiple orthogonal approaches including immunostaining and in situ hybridization. Cell cycle regression analysis confirms cluster identity is independent of proliferation state.

results.result: Two resident macrophage subpopulations (hbaa+ Mac 2 and timp4.3+ Mac 3) were identified as regeneration-associated clusters that are enriched only in regenerative hearts and barely recover after clodronate treatment. Mac 2 expresses hemoglobin genes and ROS-regulating genes (romo1, prdx2, hmox1a), while Mac 3 expresses cd74, spi1a, and timp4.3, suggesting functions in ROS homeostasis, inflammatory resolution, and ECM remodeling. These resident macrophages show low ccr2 expression, suggesting embryonic rather than monocyte-derived origin.
results.evaluation: The identification of Mac 2 and Mac 3 is supported by multiple lines of evidence: cell proportion analysis showing enrichment in regenerative conditions (Figure 3B-C), ISH validation of marker genes hbaa1 and timp4.3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and functional gene expression profiles (Figure 4, Table 1). The low ccr2 expression and proliferative capacity support the resident macrophage designation, consistent with established macrophage biology.

results.result: Macrophage clusters exhibited alternative activation patterns between regenerative and non-regenerative conditions. Under regenerative conditions, Mac 1 expressed tissue-repairing genes (vegfaa/bb, lrp1ab, elmo1, fn1a) while Mac 2 and 3 expressed M2 markers (arg2, mrc1b). Under non-regenerative conditions, Mac 1, 4, 5 expressed inflammatory genes (il1b, tnfb, ifngr2) and chemokines for neutrophil recruitment, suggesting that circulation-recruited macrophages exhibit distinct functional polarization toward continuous inflammation upon macrophage pre-depletion.
results.evaluation: The alternative activation patterns are well-documented through condition-enriched DEG analysis (Figure 4), GO enrichment analysis, and M1/M2 marker expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). The functional interpretation is supported by established macrophage polarization biology and consistent with the observed neutrophil retention phenotype. However, the causal relationship between macrophage polarization and neutrophil retention is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Two neutrophil clusters (Neu 1 and Neu 2) showed distinct functional profiles. Neu 1, enriched in regenerative conditions, expressed necroptosis genes (fth1a, caspa, hmgb1a) and granule genes (lyz, npsn, mmp13a.1, mmp9), functioning in debris clearance and programmed cell death for self-clearance. Neu 2, enriched in macrophage-delayed conditions, expressed inflammatory cytokines (il1b, tnfb), phagosome-related genes (ncf1, ncf2), and chemotaxis genes (cxcr1, atf3), functioning in inflammatory propagation and recruitment of more inflammatory cells.
results.evaluation: The neutrophil heterogeneity is supported by cluster-specific gene expression (Figure 4, Table 1), cell proportion analysis (Figure 3D), and direct comparison between clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). The functional interpretations align with established neutrophil biology regarding programmed cell death and inflammatory resolution. The correlation between Neu 2 enrichment and neutrophil retention in CL-treated hearts provides supporting evidence for the proposed functions.

results.result: Ligand-receptor interaction analysis revealed that resident macrophages Mac 2 and 3 regulate neutrophil migration and resolution through multiple pathways. Under regenerative conditions, macrophages signal neutrophil recruitment via C3-integrin and AFDN-JAM-A interactions at 3 dpci, and promote neutrophil reverse migration and phagocytic clearance via HMGB1-CXCR4, ECM remodeling (ADAMs, COL1A1, FN1, TIMP2), and MFGE8-ITGAV axis at 7 dpci. Under non-regenerative conditions, macrophages propagate inflammation via IL15, IL16, TNF, and neutrophils trigger NOTCH2 signaling promoting M1 macrophage polarization, leading to neutrophil retention and chronic inflammation.
results.evaluation: The ligand-receptor interaction analysis (Figure 5) identifies potential cell-cell communication pathways based on gene expression patterns, but these are computational predictions rather than experimentally validated interactions. While the predicted interactions are biologically plausible and supported by cited literature, the actual functional significance of these specific ligand-receptor pairs in zebrafish cardiac regeneration requires experimental validation through perturbation studies. The correlation with neutrophil retention phenotypes provides circumstantial support but not direct evidence of causality.

results.result: Pseudotemporal trajectory analysis revealed four distinct macrophage polarization routes from resident Mac 3: Route I to Mac 1 (iron homeostasis, angiogenesis), Route II to MN (pro-inflammatory, with more macrophage-like cells in regenerative hearts and neutrophil-like cells in non-regenerative hearts), Route III to Mac 5 via Mac 4, 6, 7 (oxidative stress response), and Route IV to Mac 2 (most expanded in regenerative conditions). Gene expression along pseudotime showed early enrichment of phagocytosis and complement genes, followed by lysosomal capacity enhancement, then diverse functions including oxygen transport (hbba1, hbba2) and cell proliferation, and finally neutrophil-specific genes.
results.evaluation: The pseudotemporal trajectory analysis (Figure 6A) using Monocle3 provides a coherent framework for understanding macrophage differentiation dynamics. The four routes are well-defined with distinct gene expression patterns (Figure 6C) and functional annotations supported by GO analysis. The observation that Route IV (Mac 3 to Mac 2) is absent in CL-treated hearts (Figure 6B) correlates with the loss of Mac 2 in non-regenerative conditions. However, trajectory analysis represents computational inference of developmental relationships rather than direct lineage tracing, so the actual differentiation pathways require experimental validation.

results.result: Functional validation using resident macrophage-deficient model (−8d_CL and −1m_CL) demonstrated that pre-depleting resident macrophages before cardiac injury significantly impairs heart regeneration without affecting overall macrophage recruitment from circulation. Resident macrophage-deficient hearts exhibited defects in revascularization, increased neutrophil retention, reduced cardiomyocyte density in border zones, increased TUNEL-positive cells, and larger unresolved scar tissues at 30 dpci. The regenerative defects persisted even one month after CL treatment, indicating that resident macrophages cannot be functionally replaced by circulating/monocyte-derived macrophages.
results.evaluation: The functional validation experiments provide strong evidence through multiple complementary assays: flow cytometry confirming macrophage depletion and recovery (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), qPCR and ISH confirming loss of Mac 2/3 markers (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D), and quantitative assessment of regeneration parameters including revascularization (Figure 7A), neutrophil retention (Figure 7B), cardiomyocyte proliferation and density (Figure 7C), cell death (Figure 7D), and scar resolution (Figure 7E). The −1m_CL experiment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) provides critical evidence that the defects are not due to transient macrophage depletion. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate sample sizes. The observation of macrophage overshoot in −8d_CL hearts suggests compensatory recruitment but functional inadequacy.

results.result: Mechanistic investigation revealed that resident macrophages accelerate cardiac repair partly through heme clearance via hmox1a expression. Hmox1a+ macrophages with Mac 2-like characteristics were located in the injured area and epicardial layer in regenerative hearts but were significantly reduced in resident macrophage-deficient hearts. O-dianisidine staining showed that heme was largely cleared in PBS-control hearts at 7 dpci but accumulated excessively in resident macrophage-deficient hearts, potentially contributing to cardiomyocyte death through ROS stress.
results.evaluation: The mechanistic link between resident macrophages and heme clearance is supported by multiple lines of evidence: scRNA-seq showing hmox1a enrichment in Mac 2 (Figure 8A), ISH validation of hmox1a expression in macrophage-like cells (Figure 8B), immunostaining confirming Hmox1 expression in mpeg1:mCherry+ macrophages (Figure 8C), and O-dianisidine staining demonstrating heme accumulation in resident macrophage-deficient hearts (Figure 8D). The functional significance is supported by established knowledge about heme toxicity and hmox1a's role in heme degradation. However, the causal relationship between heme accumulation and cardiomyocyte death is inferred rather than directly demonstrated through rescue experiments.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the biological context that zebrafish exhibit robust heart regeneration ability while mammals lose this capacity postnatally, and that immune responses, particularly macrophage function, represent a major difference between regenerative and non-regenerative models. The study builds on previous work showing that delaying macrophage recruitment compromises zebrafish heart regeneration, and incorporates established knowledge about cardiac metabolism, inflammatory resolution, and cell-cell interactions during tissue repair.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout the manuscript. They provide essential context for interpreting the experimental findings and are well-supported by the cited references. The integration of prior knowledge with current findings is appropriate and helps frame the significance of the results.

results.result: Previous work by the authors established the −1d_CL macrophage-delayed model, showing that delaying macrophage recruitment impairs neutrophil resolution and heart regeneration even when macrophage numbers recover. Recent studies have identified novel macrophage subpopulations in zebrafish cardiac repair, but the overall heterogeneity and function of inflammatory cells during cardiac regeneration remained unclear, motivating the current comprehensive single-cell profiling study.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately represent prior work (primarily Lai et al., 2017) and establish the rationale for the current study. The characterization of the −1d_CL model is well-documented in the cited literature, and the identification of knowledge gaps is appropriate for motivating the research questions addressed in this manuscript.
